clue.text: Double-dealing pair confronted

parts.note: a pair is two of something
to have confronted someone is to have faced them

explanation.surface: Two people met face to face, and one of them was a cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: A two-faced person is a hypocrite who deceives, which is what double-dealing describes.

clue.text: This beetle is small, loathsome, tailless!

parts.note: wee is Scottish for small

indicators.note: an animal without a tail has lost its end, so the last letter of the word for loathsome goes

parts.note: loathsome means vile

explanation.surface: A disgusted cry about a tiny insect that is repulsive and has no tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' cuts the last letter from VILE, leaving VIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The weevil is a small snouted beetle, a pest of grain and crops.

clue.text: All the plant life belonging to Miss Macdonald

explanation.surface: The garden belongs to a woman named Macdonald.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora Macdonald was the Scottish heroine who helped Bonnie Prince Charlie escape in 1746.
explanation.definitionFit: The vegetation of a region is its flora; Flora was also the first name of the famous Jacobite heroine Macdonald.

clue.text: Daily comes about one-she'll be given the floor

indicators.note: the cleaner's word goes around, so it wraps the numeral inside

parts.note: a daily is a British cleaner who comes in every day, also called a charlady
one is I as a Roman numeral

explanation.surface: The cleaning woman arrives around one o'clock and will be allowed to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'daily' or charlady is a British term for a hired cleaning woman. 'Given the floor' means allowed to speak at a meeting, as its chair is.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman chairing a meeting decides who speaks, and is herself granted the right to address it.

clue.text: Make out record English fleet?

parts.note: a gramophone record is a disc
RN, the Royal Navy, is Britain's fleet

explanation.surface: A question whether one can make out an English fleet on record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet' looks like an adjective (quick) but stands for the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: To make out something faintly seen is to perceive or detect it.

clue.text: Out on bail in old England

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A prisoner released on bail somewhere in old England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out on bail' reads as a prisoner's release, but 'Out' is the anagram signal for ON BAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Albion is an ancient and poetic name for Britain, especially England.

clue.text: Bewildered pair left this month

indicators.note: something bewildered is confused, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A confused couple departed this month.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourth month of the year, the current one at the time of a spring puzzle.

clue.text: Bonn takes change or bills

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters of these words

explanation.surface: The German city of Bonn accepts loose coins or paper money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' looks like money, fitting bills, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bills is the American word for paper currency, the notes issued by a bank.

clue.text: 0, swimmer-what a bloomer!

parts.note: the printed zero stands for the round letter O
Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit Hero in Greek legend

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a swimmer's embarrassing mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a blunder, but here it is a flowering plant.
explanation.definitionFit: The oleander is a flowering evergreen shrub, so it is literally something that blooms.

clue.text: Ball-game requires physical education and a lot of running about

indicators.note: letters running about are moving around, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sport that needs PE skills and plenty of running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running about' sounds like the exercise of the game but rearranges A LOT into LOTA.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelota is a Basque court game in which a ball is struck against a wall.

clue.text: Jumper for a spaniel?

explanation.surface: Is a jumper suitable for a dog?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' suggests the British word for a sweater, but here it is one who leaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that leaps can be called this; the English springer is also a breed of gun dog that flushes game.

clue.text: Counter quarrel

explanation.surface: A two-word note about an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: To counter a view is to contradict it; to quarrel is to argue, and both mean to differ.

clue.text: Argentine material inside Norfolk, for example?

definitions.text: Argentine material inside Norfolk, for example?

parts.words: Argentine material inside Norfolk, for example?
parts.note: argent is silver, so silver material is what lines a cloud; a Norfolk is also a belted tweed jacket, which has fabric sewn inside it

explanation.surface: A question about fabric from Argentina found in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Argent means silver, pointing to the silver lining of a cloud. A Norfolk jacket is a belted tweed jacket; Norfolk is also an English county.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabric sewn inside a garment such as a jacket is its inner layer.

clue.text: Everyday disguise of PC in SE Atholl, perhaps

indicators.note: to disguise the words is to change their appearance by reordering their letters

explanation.surface: A police constable goes undercover in the Atholl area of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' links; a plain-clothes officer is a PC in disguise, so the surface fits the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain clothes are ordinary civilian dress rather than uniform, worn every day.

clue.text: Venomous thing in advertisement-dread its coming out?

parts.note: a puff is an exaggerated piece of publicity

indicators.note: letters coming out of their places are rearranged

explanation.surface: A dangerous creature appears in an advert, causing alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming out' rearranges DREAD into ADDER.
explanation.definitionFit: The puff adder is a highly poisonous African snake that inflates itself when threatened.

clue.text: Torpor-girl with it due to be treated

parts.note: a lass is a girl

indicators.note: something treated is processed or worked on, so its letters are reworked

explanation.surface: A tired girl with an illness is due to be treated by a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be treated' rearranges DUE into UDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lethargy and weariness, a state of physical or mental sluggishness.

clue.text: Old county table

explanation.surface: An antique table from a former Welsh county.
explanation.walkthrough: Pembrokeshire, or Pembroke, was a county in south-west Wales before 1974.
explanation.definitionFit: Pembroke is a former Welsh county; a Pembroke table is a small drop-leaf table.

clue.text: Putting number one under?

parts.note: number one means oneself, and putting someone under means sending them into a trance

explanation.surface: A golfer's question about sinking a putt in the first hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one' is slang for oneself, and to 'put under' is to induce a trance or anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Inducing a trance on oneself rather than on someone else.

clue.text: Reason for infanta's visit to nursery?

definitions.text: Reason for infanta's visit to nursery?

parts.words: Reason for infanta's visit to nursery?
parts.note: a nursery rhyme tells of the King of Spain's daughter coming to see a small tree bearing a silver nutmeg and golden pear

explanation.surface: Why a Spanish princess came to see the children's room.
explanation.walkthrough: In the rhyme 'I had a little nut tree', the King of Spain's daughter (an infanta) visits for its sake. Nursery means both children's room and plant nursery.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree that bears nuts, the one in the old rhyme the Spanish princess came to see.

clue.text: Confine enemy citizen in Bury North

parts.note: to inter is to bury

explanation.surface: Locking up a foreign national in the town of Bury North.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury is a town near Manchester, which makes the capital look like a place name.
explanation.definitionFit: In wartime, nationals of a hostile state are detained in camps, a form of detention.

clue.text: A plank on a ship

parts.note: a plank is a board

explanation.surface: A gangplank leading onto a vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on a vessel is being on deck, among the passengers or crew.

clue.text: Comic beau

explanation.surface: A funny man who is also a ladies' man.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dandy was a long-running British children's comic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dandy was a British comic; a beau, like a fop, is a man devoted to fine dress.

clue.text: Flight-path of early aircraft

parts.note: a flight is a journey or trip
a lane is a narrow path or way

explanation.surface: The route flown by a pioneering aeroplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flight-path' reads as one compound but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane with three pairs of wings stacked one above another, used in the First World War.

clue.text: General chief physician of old

parts.note: Robert E. Lee was the Confederate commander in the American Civil War

explanation.surface: A senior military officer who was once a doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a doctor, from the bloodsucking worms once used in medicine.

clue.text: Bowman, we hear, could be one

definitions.text: Bowman, we hear, could be one

parts.words: Bowman, we hear, could be one
parts.note: a person from Bow in east London, born within hearing of Bow Bells, is a true cockney of the capital

explanation.surface: An archer might, by repute, come from a certain place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowman' suggests an archer, but means a man from Bow; a cockney is traditionally born within the sound of Bow Bells, the bells of a church in east London.
explanation.definitionFit: A cockney from Bow is an inhabitant of the British capital.

clue.text: Not fairly matched in a French flat

parts.note: un is French for a
flat means even, as of a surface

explanation.surface: An unfair contest held in a French apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' suggests an apartment but means level.
explanation.definitionFit: An unequal contest is one where the sides are lopsided rather than balanced.

clue.text: Jolly sailor

explanation.surface: A cheerful seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearty' is old nautical slang for a sailor, as in 'me hearties'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jolly means cheerful and boisterous; a seaman was addressed as 'my hearty'.

clue.text: One does not forget this size of paper!

explanation.surface: A memorable sheet of paper of a particular size.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying goes that this animal never forgets. Elephant was a traditional large size of drawing paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverbial creature with a long memory; also an old large paper format.
